theory.title: What a Capacity Limit Drops
overview: A layer has four experts and sends each token to its top two. In one batch of 1,000 tokens the router makes these assignments:

setup.p: Each expert accepts assignments up to its capacity and drops the rest, as in the lesson.

prompt.p: How many assignments are dropped at capacity factor 1.2?

answer.p: Each token makes $k = 2$ assignments, so a perfectly balanced expert would receive $kT/N = 2 \times 1000 / 4 = 500$. At capacity factor 1.2 each expert accepts $C = 1.2 \times 500 = 600$. Only expert 1 is over, by 20.

The $k$ matters. Switch's formula, written for $k = 1$, would give $C = 1.2 \times 1000 / 4 = 300$ here, and all four experts would overflow: $320 + 240 + 170 + 70 = 800$ assignments dropped, two fifths of the batch's assignments.

No token skips the layer at this factor. A token's two assignments go to two different experts, and only expert 1 drops anything, so each of the 20 tokens that lose their place at expert 1 keeps its other expert.

prompt.p: At capacity factor 1.0, what is the largest number of tokens that could skip the layer entirely?

answer.p: Now $C = 500$. Expert 1 drops $620 - 500 = 120$ assignments, expert 2 drops $40$, and experts 3 and 4 drop none.

A token skips the layer only when both of its assignments are dropped, so both of its experts must be ones that drop something: it chose experts 1 and 2 and lost its place at both. Expert 2 drops only 40 assignments, so at most 40 tokens skip. All 40 can. The loads force at least $620 + 540 - 1000 = 160$ tokens to choose both experts 1 and 2, since the two experts' 1,160 assignments come from only 1,000 tokens. Suppose 40 of those tokens arrive last at both experts.
The fewest is 0, when every token dropped at expert 2 kept its other assignment. The loads alone do not say which case happens. That depends on the order in which the experts fill their buffers.

prompt.p: Find the smallest capacity factor that drops nothing. At that factor, what fraction of all the buffer slots is padding? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: Nothing is dropped once $C \ge 620$, the busiest expert's load, so the smallest factor is $620 / 500 = 1.24$. Every expert then gets 620 slots, which makes $4 \times 620 = 2480$ slots for $2000$ assignments. The other $480$ are padding:

Expert 4 alone leaves 250 of its 620 slots empty. The busiest expert sets the buffer size for all of them, so the factor that drops nothing is the largest load over the fair share, and the padding grows with the imbalance. Padding still costs memory, compute and communication, which is why balancing the router is what lets the capacity factor stay small.

theory.title: Splitting Every Expert in Four
overview: A Switch-style layer has $N = 16$ experts and sends each token to one of them. Every expert is a feed-forward network of the lesson's form, $W_2\,\sigma(W_1 \mathbf{x})$ without biases, with $d_{\text{model}} = 2048$ and $d_{\text{ff}} = 8192$. A team proposes to split every expert into four smaller ones with $d_{\text{ff}} = 2048$, which gives 64 experts holding the same expert parameters as before.

prompt.p: How many of the 64 experts must each token use to keep the expert FLOPs per token as they were? How many different sets of experts can a token then be sent to? Enter the number of sets.

answer.p: A feed-forward network costs about $4\, d_{\text{model}}\, d_{\text{ff}}$ FLOPs per token, so a small expert costs a quarter of a large one, and a token must use 4 small experts to cost what one large expert did. The parameters match too: $64 \times 2 \times 2048 \times 2048 = 16 \times 2 \times 2048 \times 8192 = 536{,}870{,}912$. Only the router grows, from $16 \times 2048$ to $64 \times 2048$ weights, which is small next to the experts.
A token can now be sent to any 4 of the 64 experts:
sets, against 16 before, for the same parameters and the same FLOPs. This is the gain in combinations that makes fine-grained experts attractive.

prompt.p: The experts are spread over 16 devices: one large expert per device before the split, and four small ones per device after it. Sending a token to an expert on another device moves the token's vector of $d_{\text{model}}$ numbers there and the expert's output vector back, in 16-bit floats of 2 bytes each. An expert on the token's own device costs nothing. Assume the router spreads tokens uniformly, so that every set of experts is equally likely. If each of a token's assignments is sent separately, how many bytes of traffic does one token cause in the split layer, on average?

answer.p: One round trip moves $2 \times 2048 \times 2 = 8192$ bytes. Each of the token's 4 experts is equally likely to be any of the 64, and 60 of those sit on other devices, so each assignment leaves the device with probability $60/64 = 15/16$. By linearity of expectation,

The layer before the split costs $\frac{15}{16} \times 8192 = 7680$ bytes per token. The split keeps the FLOPs and quadruples the all-to-all traffic, because communication grows with the number of experts each token visits.

prompt.p: A device that holds two or more of a token's experts needs the token's vector only once: it can run all of them and send back one weighted sum. With this change, how many other devices does a token's vector go to, on average? Give it to three decimal places, and say what the result means for the traffic.

answer.p: Count devices instead of assignments. A device receives the token if it holds at least one of the token's 4 experts. It holds 4 of the 64, so the token misses all of them with probability

and each of the 15 other devices receives the token with probability $0.2325$. By linearity of expectation the token goes to $15 \times 0.2325 \approx 3.488$ other devices on average, against 3.75 when every assignment travels on its own.

The traffic falls from 30,720 to about $3.488 \times 8192 \approx 28{,}573$ bytes, only 7%, and stays 3.7 times that of the layer before the split. Four experts drawn from 64 rarely share a device, so sharing a trip saves little. Cutting the traffic would need a router that confines each token's experts to a few devices, and that would give up part of the 635,376 sets from Part 1: the routing's flexibility and its traffic grow together.

theory.title: What a Top-2 Router Learns From
overview: A Mixtral-style layer sends each token to its two most probable experts and renormalizes. With router probabilities $\mathbf{g} = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z})$ over $N$ experts and chosen experts $a$ and $b$, the layer outputs

setup.tex:
\mathbf{y} = w_a\, E_a(\mathbf{x}) + w_b\, E_b(\mathbf{x}), \qquad
w_a = \frac{g_a}{g_a + g_b}, \quad w_b = \frac{g_b}{g_a + g_b} .

setup.p: Write $\mathbf{u} = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \mathbf{y}$ for the gradient that backpropagation brings to the layer's output, and assume no two logits are equal.

prompt.p: Find $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_j$ for every expert $j$, in terms of $w_a$, $w_b$, $\mathbf{u}$, $E_a(\mathbf{x})$ and $E_b(\mathbf{x})$.

answer.p: Write out the weights. The softmax denominator appears in both $g_a$ and $g_a + g_b$, so it cancels:

The weights depend on the two chosen logits and nothing else. A small change in any other logit keeps the token's top two as they were, since no logits tie, so $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_j = 0$ for every $j$ other than $a$ and $b$.
With $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)$, $\partial w_a / \partial z_a = w_a w_b$ and $\partial w_b / \partial z_a = -w_a w_b$. The expert outputs do not depend on $\mathbf{z}$, so
and by the same steps $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_b$ is its negative.

prompt.p: One token has router probabilities $\mathbf{g} = (0.10,\ 0.45,\ 0.30,\ 0.15)$ over four experts. Its chosen experts return $E_2(\mathbf{x}) = (1,\ -0.5,\ 2)$ and $E_3(\mathbf{x}) = (0.5,\ 1,\ 1)$, and $\mathbf{u} = (0.4,\ 0.2,\ -0.3)$. Find $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_2$, and say what a descent step does to the token's routing.

answer.p: The top two are experts 2 and 3, with weights $0.45 / 0.75 = 0.6$ and $0.30 / 0.75 = 0.4$, so $w_a w_b = 0.24$. The difference of the outputs is $E_2(\mathbf{x}) - E_3(\mathbf{x}) = (0.5,\ -1.5,\ 1)$, and

So $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_3 = 0.096$, and the entries for experts 1 and 4 are 0. A descent step raises $z_2$, lowers $z_3$ and leaves the other two alone, which moves weight from expert 3 to expert 2. Shifting weight between the two changes $\mathbf{y}$ along $E_2(\mathbf{x}) - E_3(\mathbf{x})$, and $\mathbf{u}$ says that direction lowers the loss.

The router learns which of its two chosen experts did better on this token, and only that. If both outputs moved by the same vector, the gradient would not change. The experts it did not choose get no signal at all.

prompt.p: A team builds an MoE layer from a trained dense model by copying its feed-forward network into all eight experts and adding a new router, then keeps training with the task loss. Leave the balance loss out. What gradient does the router receive at the first step? Does it stay that way?

answer.p: At the first step every expert computes the same function, so $E_a(\mathbf{x}) = E_b(\mathbf{x})$ for every token and every pair. By Part 1 every token's router gradient is $w_a w_b\, \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{0} = 0$, and the router does not move.

It does not stay that way, because the experts drift apart. Expert $a$'s parameters receive the gradient of $\mathbf{u} \cdot E_a(\mathbf{x})$, scaled by $w_a$, summed over the tokens routed to it. Each expert sees its own tokens with its own weights, so after one step the copies differ. From then on $E_a(\mathbf{x}) - E_b(\mathbf{x})$ is nonzero and the router gets a gradient. It is small at first, in proportion to how far the experts have drifted, so the router starts out learning slowly.

The balance loss would give the router a gradient from the first step, since its gradient flows through the probabilities directly. But that gradient only spreads the tokens evenly. It says nothing about which expert suits which token. For that the router needs experts that differ.

theory.title: How Low the Balance Loss Goes
overview: A layer with two experts sends each token to the expert with the higher router probability, and a token whose two probabilities are equal may go to either one. The layer adds the lesson's auxiliary loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha N \sum_i f_i P_i$, here with $N = 2$.

prompt.p: In one batch a fifth of the tokens go to expert 1, each with router probabilities $(0.95,\ 0.05)$, and the rest go to expert 2, each with $(0.45,\ 0.55)$. Find $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} / \alpha$.

answer.p: The token fractions are $f = (0.2,\ 0.8)$. The mean probabilities are
so

Expert 2 receives four times as many tokens as expert 1, and the loss is still below its balanced value of 1. The confident tokens on expert 1 lift $P_1$ far above $f_1$, and $P_1$ carries the smaller of the two weights in the loss.

prompt.p: Find the largest number $m$ such that $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} / \alpha \ge m$ for every batch, prove the bound, and describe batches that come as close to $m$ as you like.

answer.p: Write $a = f_1$, so $f_2 = 1 - a$, and $p = P_1$, so $P_2 = 1 - p$:

Take $a \le \tfrac12$ first. The loss falls as $p$ rises, so look for the largest $p$ a batch with this $a$ allows. A token that went to expert 2 gave expert 1 a probability of at most $\tfrac12$, and a token that went to expert 1 gave it at most 1. So
and
For $a \ge \tfrac12$, swap the names of the experts: the same argument with $1 - a$ in place of $a$ gives the same bound. So $m = 7/8 = 0.875$.

Equality needs $a = \tfrac14$ and both inequalities for $p$ tight: a quarter of the tokens go to expert 1 with probability 1 for it, and the other three quarters sit exactly at $(\tfrac12,\ \tfrac12)$ and go to expert 2. A softmax never outputs exactly 1, but probabilities $(1 - \epsilon,\ \epsilon)$ and $(\tfrac12,\ \tfrac12)$ get within any distance of $0.875$. The minimum is a split of one quarter to three quarters, not the even split.

prompt.p: Training treats $f$ as a constant and lets the gradient flow through $P$. For a token in Part 1's batch that went to expert 2, compute $(T/\alpha)\, \partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} / \partial z_1$, where $T$ is the number of tokens in the batch and $z_1$ is the token's logit for expert 1. Then say which way a descent step pushes the routing of Part 1's batch, toward balance or away from it, given that its loss is already below the balanced value.

answer.p: Only the token's own probabilities depend on its logits, through $P_i = \frac1T \sum_t g_{ti}$. With two experts, $\partial g_1 / \partial z_1 = g_1 g_2$ and $\partial g_2 / \partial z_1 = -g_1 g_2$, so

For the token at $(0.45,\ 0.55)$ that is $\frac{\alpha}{T} \times 2 \times (0.2 - 0.8) \times 0.2475 = -0.297\,\frac{\alpha}{T}$, and $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} / \partial z_2$ is its negative.

Descent raises $z_1$ and lowers $z_2$ for every token, since $f_1 - f_2 < 0$ for the whole batch. It moves probability toward expert 1, the expert with the smaller $f$, which is the direction of balance, even though the loss is already below the balanced value. The push is strongest where $g_1 g_2$ is largest, near the tie: the tokens at $(0.45,\ 0.55)$ get $0.2475$ out of a possible $0.25$, while the confident tokens at $(0.95,\ 0.05)$ get $0.0475$, less than a fifth as much.

The direction is right, but the gradient cannot see how many tokens a step will move across the tie. In this batch all the tokens on expert 2 are identical, so they cross together: $f$ jumps from $(0.2,\ 0.8)$ to $(1,\ 0)$, the gradient reverses, and the routing swings back and forth. Tokens with different margins cross a few at a time, and then the fractions can settle near $(0.5,\ 0.5)$.

The value and the gradient disagree because they answer different questions. Part 2 minimized over $f$ and $P$ together. Training holds $f$ fixed, and with $f$ fixed the loss is linear in $P$ with weights $f$, so it always falls by moving probability toward the expert with the smaller $f$. The loss does its work through that gradient. Its value is not a measure of balance, which is why the fractions $f$ themselves are the thing to watch.

theory.title: Where the Routing Bias Settles
overview: A layer with two experts sends each token to the expert with the larger biased score $s_i + b_i$ and balances its load with the bias rule from the lesson: after each step, an expert that received more than half of the tokens has its bias lowered by $\gamma = 0.004$, and one that received less has its bias raised by $\gamma$. Write $\Delta = s_1 - s_2$ for a token's score difference. In every batch $\Delta$ is spread uniformly between $-0.2$ and $0.6$, and the batches are large enough that each expert's share of the tokens equals its probability. Both biases start at 0.

prompt.p: After how many updates do the two experts receive equal shares of the tokens?

answer.p: A token goes to expert 1 when $s_1 + b_1 > s_2 + b_2$, that is when $\Delta > c$ with $c = b_2 - b_1$. Only this difference of the biases matters. With $\Delta$ uniform on $[-0.2,\ 0.6]$, expert 1's share is

At the start $c = 0$ and expert 1 gets $0.75$ of the tokens. Each update then lowers $b_1$ by $0.004$ and raises $b_2$ by $0.004$, so $c$ grows by $0.008$. The shares are equal when $(0.6 - c)/0.8 = 0.5$, at $c = 0.2$, the median of $\Delta$. That takes $0.2 / 0.008 = 25$ updates. After that neither expert is over its share and the biases stop moving. With batches of finite size the shares would wobble, and $c$ would hover within a step or two of $0.2$.

prompt.p: Once the shares are equal, what fraction of all tokens goes to the expert with the lower score?

answer.p: The tokens with $0 < \Delta < 0.2$ score higher on expert 1 but have $\Delta < c$, so they go to expert 2. They make up $0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25$ of the tokens: a third of the $0.75$ that prefer expert 1. No token that prefers expert 2 moves.

These are the tokens with the weakest preference. The bias moves one boundary shared by every token, and the tokens it moves are the ones that sat closest to it, each giving up at most 0.2 in score. Their gate weights still come from their scores without the bias, so the layer weighs expert 2's output by what the token really scored there.

prompt.p: In another layer every token has $\Delta = 0.3$ exactly. Describe what the bias rule does, starting from biases of 0, and say whether the two experts' loads ever balance.

answer.p: Every token makes the same comparison, $0.3 > c$, so in every step all the tokens go to the same expert. For the first 38 steps $c$ is below $0.3$: expert 1 gets every token, and $c$ climbs by $0.008$ a step to $0.304$. In step 39 every token goes to expert 2, and the update brings $c$ back to $0.296$. In step 40 every token goes to expert 1 again, and so on: from step 39 on, the experts take turns receiving the whole batch.

The loads never balance within a step. They balance only on average over two steps, which does nothing for the device that must hold a full batch's worth of assignments in one step, and a smaller $\gamma$ only makes the swings start later. The bias can balance a layer only by moving the tokens nearest the boundary to the other expert, and that needs tokens whose preferences differ. Here the scores do not tell the tokens apart, so the problem lies with the router, and no choice of bias can fix it.
